KEY MESSAGE 1...Blustery and cloudy conditions today give way 
to a pleasant day Sunday.

Gusty winds continue today as southern New England remains in a
tighter pressure gradient from the low moving further northeast
into Atlantic Canada and high pressure building to the south. 
Expecting skies to remain cloudy today too due to trapped 
moisture at the surface under an 850mb inversion. High 
temperatures cool a little today compared to yesterday as weak 
CAA works it's way into New England. 925mb temperatures look to 
remain above freezing, translating to surface temperatures near 
50 this afternoon.

Sunday should be the better day of the weekend as ridging from 
the high over the southern Atlantic pushes a slightly drier 
airmass into southern New England. Afternoon highs Sunday 
slightly warmer than today thanks to clearing skies and full 
sun... likely in the mid 50s across the region.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Another storm system brings periods of heavy 
rain and potentially strong winds Monday, followed by blustery 
and cooler conditions Monday night into Tuesday.

Weak high pressure moves offshore Sunday night as a rather 
robust, negatively tilted mid-level trough approaches southern 
New England early Monday. While the primary area of low pressure
tracks across the eastern Great Lakes and northeastward along 
the St. Lawrence River Valley toward Montreal and Quebec City, 
the 00z guidance continues to suggest the development of a 
secondary low over southern New England. As previous forecasters
have noted, the strength and eventual track of this secondary 
low will have implications for both rainfall amounts and the 
magnitude of post- frontal northwest winds.

A rather striking feature in the 00z RRFS is a well-defined 
fine line that races across southern New England between 6 and 
11 AM Monday. Given the strong forcing associated with the 
shortwave energy and 925 mb winds on the order of 50-60 knots, 
there is some concern for stronger winds aloft mixing down to 
the surface with the passage of this line. Additionally, PWATs 
are once again elevated, around 1.3 inches, with forecast 
soundings depicting warm cloud depths of 8-10 kft. This would 
support the potential for heavy downpours, which, combined with 
potentially strong wind gusts, could result in poor driving 
conditions during the Monday morning commute.

Despite the elevated PWATs, this is a rather fast-moving 
system, and rainfall amounts will be considerably less than what
fell on Thanksgiving. The GEFS depicts virtually no probability
of 24-hour rainfall exceeding an inch, while the ECMWF ensemble
depicts probabilities of 20-40 percent across RI and 
southeastern MA. For now, anticipating a widespread half inch to
an inch of rainfall. Given the 2-3+ inches of rainfall that 
fell across portions of RI and eastern MA on Thanksgiving, 
additional rainfall could result in some of the already swollen 
rivers rising back into action stage, if not minor flood stage. 
Of particular interest are the Pawtuxet River at Cranston and 
the Taunton River near Bridgewater, both of which have 
experienced flooding following the Thanksgiving storm. Much of 
this will depend on how quickly river levels recede over the 
weekend.

Of equal concern is the potential for strong post-frontal 
northwest winds Monday afternoon into the evening. Strong cold 
air advection may allow for mixing as high as 850 mb, where 
winds are on the order of 50-70 knots. The areas of greatest 
concern at this time are the northern Worcester Hills and 
Berkshires, where wind headlines may eventually be needed. The 
ECMWF ensemble depicts a 30-50 percent probability of gusts 
exceeding 50 knots (58 mph) across the Berkshires, with 
probabilities exceeding 90 percent for gusts greater than 34 
knots (40 mph). The GEFS is considerably less robust, with 
little to no support for 50+ knot gusts and probabilities of 
20-50 percent for gusts exceeding 34 knots. Given the 
differences in the ensemble guidance and that this event is 
still several days out, this certainly bears watching. Over the 
waters, another round of gale to strong gale-force gusts appears
possible Monday into Monday night.

A rather mild day Monday with highs in the mid 50s to around 
60. Winds gradually diminish by early Tuesday morning as 1025+ 
mb high pressure builds in from the southwest. Seasonable 
temperatures Monday night with lows on either side of freezing. 
Given the elevated winds behind the front, most road surfaces 
should have an opportunity to dry out, limiting the potential 
for refreezing.
